criteria.rationale: Pass: none of the delivered browser tests sleeps for a fixed time before asserting. Each one waits for observable state. Which tests drive a browser: vitest.config.ts runs tests/unit only, under jsdom. vitest.integration.config.ts runs tests/integration and tests/e2e under node. Only those two folders contain browser tests. The only test that drives Playwright itself is in tests/integration/inspect.test.ts; it launches chromium at line 125. In tests/unit/scripts.test.ts, captureSteps gets a plain mock object whose waitForTimeout only records an event, so no browser runs there. The one test that drives a page directly is 'removes the exiting scene host…' (inspect.test.ts:252-265). It calls page.waitForSelector('[data-step-count]'), presses ArrowRight, then polls with page.waitForFunction until the scene-host count is 1, with a 5000 ms timeout. Only after that wait does it read locator.count(), and it uses that count purely as an assertion, not as a wait. Every other browser test starts the inspect or verify scripts as child processes through run() (support.ts:48-56). run() resolves on the child's 'close' event, so each test waits for the process to finish before checking its exit code, output, or files. This covers the INT-002 helper tests, the bootstrap tests, and the e2e verify tests. None of the quoted test files calls waitForTimeout, setTimeout, or any other sleep while waiting. The setTimeout calls in the inspect fixture (line 53) and in the verify-failures fault edits (lines 73-91) are code written into the app under test, not waits in the test. Panel A and panel B: their reasons match the cited code, so I rule their pass. Panel C: C fails the 'captures only after the transition settles' test (inspect.test.ts:222-250) because it passes --settle 1200 and --settle 50. That reason does not decide this criterion. Those flags set the delivered helper's own settle interval; they are the feature the test is checking, not a sleep the test uses to wait for a transition before asserting. The test itself waits for each child process to close (run() → 'close'). It then makes deterministic assertions on the screenshot pixels and on the capture-log timing (capturedAt − navigatedAt ≥ 1200). Whether the helper should use a fixed settle delay belongs to the helper's own criteria, not to whether the tests wait on state.

votes.rationale: The verifier does reserve its own ephemeral port and passes --strictPort. But readiness comes only from HTTP polling of that port, and the child's liveness is sampled before each fetch. waitReady checks child.exitCode and then fetches, and accepts any res.ok. result.rationale: I'm ruling with Judge B. The verifier fails real render and transition faults, and the e2e regressions for them exist: 'render fault that breaks step 6' and 'transition that does not advance the step index'. However, the review guidance says to fail when the transition check turns a non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison, and gives the first step as the example. In scripts/verify.mjs, waitForIndex maps only a null attribute to null and passes every other raw string through Number(raw). An empty or whitespace data-step-index ('' or ' ') becomes 0, so actual === expected holds when i === 0. The loop in renderSample then treats step 1 as reached, even though the hook is non-numeric. The requirement that a missing or non-numeric hook is never counted as progress is therefore unmet. Judges A and C point to indexProblem rejecting null and NaN, and to !(count > 0) guarding the step count. Both observations are accurate, but neither decides the criterion. indexProblem runs only when waitForIndex has not already returned, and an empty string never becomes NaN or null: it becomes 0 and returns early at the equality check. engineering-quality.rationale: Pass: none of the delivered browser tests sleeps for a fixed time before asserting. Each one waits for observable state. Which tests drive a browser: vitest.config.ts runs tests/unit only, under jsdom. vitest.integration.config.ts runs tests/integration and tests/e2e under node. Only those two folders contain browser tests. The only test that drives Playwright itself is in tests/integration/inspect.test.ts; it launches chromium at line 125. In tests/unit/scripts.test.ts, captureSteps gets a plain mock object whose waitForTimeout only records an event, so no browser runs there. The one test that drives a page directly is 'removes the exiting scene host…' (inspect.test.ts:252-265). It calls page.waitForSelector('[data-step-count]'), presses ArrowRight, then polls with page.waitForFunction until the scene-host count is 1, with a 5000 ms timeout. Only after that wait does it read locator.count(), and it uses that count purely as an assertion, not as a wait. Every other browser test starts the inspect or verify scripts as child processes through run() (support.ts:48-56). run() resolves on the child's 'close' event, so each test waits for the process to finish before checking its exit code, output, or files. This covers the INT-002 helper tests, the bootstrap tests, and the e2e verify tests. None of the quoted test files calls waitForTimeout, setTimeout, or any other sleep while waiting. The setTimeout calls in the inspect fixture (line 53) and in the verify-failures fault edits (lines 73-91) are code written into the app under test, not waits in the test. Panel A and panel B: their reasons match the cited code, so I rule their pass. Panel C: C fails the 'captures only after the transition settles' test (inspect.test.ts:222-250) because it passes --settle 1200 and --settle 50. That reason does not decide this criterion. Those flags set the delivered helper's own settle interval; they are the feature the test is checking, not a sleep the test uses to wait for a transition before asserting. The test itself waits for each child process to close (run() → 'close'). It then makes deterministic assertions on the screenshot pixels and on the capture-log timing (capturedAt − navigatedAt ≥ 1200). Whether the helper should use a fixed settle delay belongs to the helper's own criteria, not to whether the tests wait on state.

scene-kit.rationale: Mode and index are separate useState values in usePresentationNav. toggleMode only flips the mode, and the 'p' key maps to the toggle-mode action. Presentation renders steps[index] in both modes, so the current step is unchanged.

scene-kit.rationale: actionForKey maps ArrowRight, Space and PageDown to next, and ArrowLeft and PageUp to prev. The window keydown handler runs the action, which makes one clamped step.
evidence: usePresentationNav.ts actionForKey cases.
onKeyDown calls run(action), which calls next() or prev().

scene-kit.rationale: touchstart and touchend listeners compute dx and dy and pass them to classifySwipe. It returns 'next' for dx<0 and 'prev' for dx>0, after a 40px threshold. The result is run through the same next() and prev() functions as the keyboard, which move one clamped step.
evidence: classifySwipe: `dx < 0 ? 'next' : 'prev'`.
onTouchEnd computes the deltas and calls run(action).
constants.ts SWIPE_THRESHOLD = 40.

scene-kit.rationale: Each progress button calls onGoTo(i) for its own step. Each TOC entry calls onGoTo(era.firstIndex), and groupEras records the first step index of each consecutive era. Presentation wires onGoTo to goTo.
evidence: Footer.tsx progress buttons onClick={() => onGoTo(i)}.
Toc.tsx onClick={() => onGoTo(era.firstIndex)}.
eras.ts groupEras firstIndex.
Presentation.tsx passes goTo as onGoTo.

scene-kit.rationale: The active progress button and the active TOC entry both set aria-current='step' and data-presentation-active='true'. The sample CSS targets that hook.

presentation.css styles [data-presentation-active='true'].

scene-kit.rationale: onKeyDown returns early, before preventDefault and actionForKey, when the event target is within an interactive element. The INTERACTIVE selector covers button, a[href], input, select, textarea and others. All the controls the kit renders are buttons or an anchor, so they keep their own keys.
evidence: INTERACTIVE selector.
`if (isInteractiveTarget(e.target)) return` precedes actionForKey and preventDefault.
Footer and Toc controls are button elements; Attribution is an a[href].

scene-kit.rationale: prev goes through clampIndex(i-1, count), which floors at 0. The Prev button is also disabled on the first step.
evidence: usePresentationNav.ts prev and clampIndex.
Footer.tsx Prev disabled={index === 0}.

scene-kit.rationale: next goes through clampIndex(i+1, count), which caps at count-1. The Next button is also disabled on the last step.
evidence: usePresentationNav.ts next and clampIndex.
Footer.tsx Next disabled={index === steps.length - 1}.

scene-kit.rationale: computeFitScale is one factor, max(MIN_SCALE, min(availW/canvasW, availH/canvasH)), computed from the space left after chrome is reserved. Stage sizes its box to that area and applies the same scale to a fixed-size inner canvas, so the composition does not reflow. At the reference viewports the scaled canvas fits inside the stage area. 1280×720 browse: avail 1068×494, scale 1.2136, canvas 1068×461. 1280×720 present: avail 1248×568, scale 1.418, canvas 1248×539. 390×844: no TOC, width 358, scale 0.4068, canvas 358×155, which fits within avail heights of 618 (browse) and 692 (present). The 0.2 floor is not reached.
evidence: useFitScale.ts availableSpace and computeFitScale.
Stage.tsx: stage box uses avail; inner canvas has fixed width/height and `transform: scale(scale)`.
constants.ts STAGE_LAYOUT browse {56,170,16}, present {56,96,16}; TOC_WIDTH 180; WIDE_BREAKPOINT 900.
Footer and Header heights equal the reserved STAGE_LAYOUT values.

scene-kit.rationale: DESIGN_W = 880 and DESIGN_H = 380 feed DEFAULT_CANVAS. Stage uses it as the default `canvas` prop, and the rendered canvas and inner element take their width and height from it.
evidence: constants.ts DESIGN_W/DESIGN_H.
useFitScale.ts DEFAULT_CANVAS.
Stage.tsx `canvas = DEFAULT_CANVAS`.
stage.test.tsx asserts 880px and 380px.

scene-kit.rationale: entityProps gives every entity primitive layout, a layoutId equal to the stable entity id, and a LAYOUT_T transition. Stage wraps scenes in LayoutGroup, so a persisting entity animates in place.

scene-kit.rationale: Stage uses AnimatePresence in its default sync mode, so the outgoing and incoming hosts stay mounted together. The outgoing host is position:absolute, so it is out of layout flow. The entity primitives set no initial opacity and no entrance delay, so a shared-id entity is not hidden.
evidence: Stage.tsx: <LayoutGroup><AnimatePresence initial={false}> with no mode='wait'. The host motion.div is position:absolute and crossfades over ENTER_T.
geometry.ts entityProps has no initial and no delay. Box sets no initial opacity.
The Appear fade-in with delay is opt-in and is not part of the primitives.
stage.test.tsx asserts two hosts and two 'e' entities coexist when hosts differ.

evidence: constants.ts: LAYOUT_T = 0.5 and ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T.

scene-kit.rationale: The kit provides Appear with an exit animation and exports AnimatePresence as Presence. The sample renders all its entities through Group, which wraps Appear in Presence.

scene-kit.rationale: hostKey returns the same key for adjacent steps with the same groupKey and Scene. Stage keys its host on that value, so the existing Scene instance receives the new payload.

scene-kit.rationale: In a grouped scene the host and Scene instance persist, so continuing children are not remounted. The kit primitives have no newcomer fade. The fade lives only in the opt-in Appear, and a continuing entity is not wrapped in a fresh one.
evidence: hostKey and the Stage key keep the same instance across grouped updates.
Box and Arrow set no initial opacity. Appear is separate.
TalkScene Group keeps a stable Appear key per group.
stage.test.tsx tracks the continuing entity's opacity through navigation and asserts it never leaves '' or '1' and has no Appear ancestor.

scene-kit.rationale: Entities are placed at literal absolute canvas coordinates inside absolutely positioned layers. Overlap and stacking is preserved, and morphs use layoutId rather than flow layout.
evidence: geometry.ts placeStyle: position absolute with the at coordinates.

entities.ts has overlapping rects: the tray, the cards, the verify chips and the full-canvas frame.

evidence: actionForKey maps ArrowRight, Space and PageDown to next, and ArrowLeft and PageUp to prev; those callbacks add or subtract one.

scene-kit.rationale: Progress indicators jump to their step, and ToC entries jump to their era's first step.

scene-kit.rationale: Forward navigation cannot move beyond the last step.

scene-kit.rationale: The authored canvas scales uniformly within the actual stage bounds at both reference viewports and modes.

votes.rationale: Props are typed from HTMLMotionProps<'div'>, and kit-only props such as at, Icon and entity are destructured off the DOM. But Box and Arrow spread {...entityProps(...)} before {...rest}, so a caller's rest props are applied afterwards and can override the kit's identity hooks (data-presentation-box, data-presentation-entity, layout, transition). The requirement says identity hooks must be applied after caller props. The runtime spread is unprotected even though 'id' and 'layoutId' are omitted from the types.

src/presentation-kit/nodes/Arrow.tsx: {...entityProps(entity,'arrow')} {...rest}
src/presentation-kit/nodes/geometry.ts entityProps returns layoutId, data-presentation-<hook> and data-presentation-entity

votes.rationale: Props are typed from the element (HTMLMotionProps<'div'>, HTMLAttributes), and kit-only props such as entity, at, Icon, z and delay are destructured out of the DOM spread. But the kit does not apply its identity hooks after caller props. Box and Arrow spread `{...entityProps(entity,'box')}` before `{...rest}`. entityProps supplies data-presentation-box, data-presentation-entity, layout and transition. A caller can therefore override those attributes, so they are not applied after caller props. Appear sets data-presentation-appear before {...rest}, and SceneLayer sets data-presentation-scene-layer before {...rest}, so those hooks are overridable too.
evidence: src/presentation-kit/nodes/Box.tsx: <motion.div {...entityProps(entity,'box')} {...rest} style=...>
src/presentation-kit/nodes/Arrow.tsx: {...entityProps(entity,'arrow')} then {...rest}
src/presentation-kit/nodes/Appear.tsx: data-presentation-appear="" then {...rest}
src/presentation-kit/nodes/SceneLayer.tsx: data-presentation-scene-layer="" then {...rest}

votes.rationale: Public primitives spread caller props after kit identity hooks, permitting those hooks to be overwritten.

first_results.rationale: I'm ruling with Judge B. The verifier fails real render and transition faults, and the e2e regressions for them exist: 'render fault that breaks step 6' and 'transition that does not advance the step index'. However, the review guidance says to fail when the transition check turns a non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison, and gives the first step as the example. In scripts/verify.mjs, waitForIndex maps only a null attribute to null and passes every other raw string through Number(raw). An empty or whitespace data-step-index ('' or ' ') becomes 0, so actual === expected holds when i === 0. The loop in renderSample then treats step 1 as reached, even though the hook is non-numeric. The requirement that a missing or non-numeric hook is never counted as progress is therefore unmet. Judges A and C point to indexProblem rejecting null and NaN, and to !(count > 0) guarding the step count. Both observations are accurate, but neither decides the criterion. indexProblem runs only when waitForIndex has not already returned, and an empty string never becomes NaN or null: it becomes 0 and returns early at the equality check. The count guard covers only data-step-count, not data-step-index. Judge C's unit cases in tests/unit/scripts.test.ts call indexProblem with null and NaN directly and never exercise the Number('') conversion in waitForIndex.
evidence: scripts/verify.mjs:133-143 waitForIndex: actual = raw === null ? null : Number(raw); if (actual === expected) return. Number('') === 0, so an empty, non-numeric data-step-index satisfies expe…
scripts/verify.mjs:99-103 indexProblem rejects only null and NaN, and it is reached only after the early return has failed, so it never sees the empty-string case.
scripts/verify.mjs:173-178: the step loop calls waitForIndex(page, i) for i = 0 and counts the step as passed when no problem comes back.
tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts:98-113 cover a thrown render fault and a stalled transition, but no test covers a non-numeric or empty step-index hook.

The verifier fails real render and transition faults, and the e2e regressions for them exist: 'render fault that breaks step 6' and 'transition that does not advance the step index'. However, the review guidance says to fail when the transition check turns a non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison, and gives the first step as the example. In scripts/verify.mjs, waitForIndex maps only a null attribute to null and passes every other raw string through Number(raw). An empty or whitespace data-step-index ('' or ' ') becomes 0, so actual === expected holds when i === 0. The loop in renderSample then treats step 1 as reached, even though the hook is non-numeric. The requirement that a missing or non-numeric hook is never counted as progress is therefore unmet. Judges A and C point to indexProblem rejecting null and NaN, and to !(count > 0) guarding the step count. Both observations are accurate, but neither decides the criterion. indexProblem runs only when waitForIndex has not already returned, and an empty string never becomes NaN or null: it becomes 0 and returns early at the equality check. The count guard covers only data-step-count, not data-step-index. Judge C's unit cases in tests/unit/scripts.test.ts call indexProblem with null and NaN directly and never exercise the Number('') conversion in waitForIndex.

first_results.rationale: The browser-driving tests are in tests/integration and tests/e2e; vitest.integration.config.ts is the browser/subprocess config. The unit tests run under jsdom, set at vitest.config.ts:6, so they do not drive a browser. Only one test drives Playwright directly: 'removes the exiting scene host…' in tests/integration/inspect.test.ts. It waits with page.waitForSelector('[data-step-count]'), presses ArrowRight, and then polls with page.waitForFunction until exactly one scene host remains (5 s timeout). Its locator count() runs only after that wait and is used as an assertion, not as a wait. Every other browser test runs the inspect or verify script through run() in support.ts. run() resolves on the child process 'close' event, so assertions start only after the observable process exit and the files it wrote. None of these tests calls waitForTimeout, setTimeout-as-sleep, or any other fixed delay in test code. The setTimeout calls in inspect.test.ts:53 and verify-failures.test.ts belong to the fixture app code being tested. Judges A and B are right. Judge C's reason does not decide the criterion. The 'captures only after the transition settles' test (lines 222-250) passes --settle 1200 or 50 to the script under test. The test itself waits only for the subprocess to exit, then checks the resulting screenshots and capture log. The page.waitForTimeout(settleMs) at inspect-presentation.mjs:176 belongs to the shipped helper's documented settle feature, which the test is checking. It is not a sleep the test uses in place of waiting for state. The helper also polls data-step-index before capturing (waitForIndex, lines 157-165).
